k-11.1-plan-contents-pim.title: 11.1 risk management plan (continued): probability and impact matrix and scoring, reporting formats, tracking
k-11.1-plan-contents-pim.notes: Probability and impact matrix: prioritisation rules may be set by the organisation in advance (OPAs) or tailored to the project; threats and opportunities share a common matrix using negative impact definitions for threats and positive ones for opportunities; descriptive terms (very high to very low) or numbers; numeric probability x impact gives a probability-impact score that ranks risks within each priority level. Figure 11-5 example: probability scale Very High 0.90, High 0.70, Medium 0.50, Low 0.30, Very Low 0.10; impact scale Very Low 0.05, Low 0.10, Moderate 0.20, High 0.40, Very High 0.80; each cell = product (e.g., 0.90 x 0.80 = 0.72; 0.50 x 0.40 = 0.20; 0.10 x 0.05 = 0.005 shown as 0.01); the threat half mirrors the opportunity half. Shading as rendered marks three priority zones: darkest (high) cells 0.72, 0.36, 0.56, 0.28, 0.40, 0.24; mid-grey (medium) cells such as 0.18, 0.09, 0.14, 0.10, 0.20, 0.12, 0.08; unshaded (low) the remainder - zone boundaries are an example, not a rule. Reporting formats: how outcomes are documented, analysed and communicated, incl. content and format of the risk register and risk report. Tracking: how risk activities are recorded and risk processes audited.

k-11.2-identify-risks.title: 11.2 Identify Risks: participants, risk statements, techniques (checklists, assumption and constraint analysis, SWOT, prompt lists - PESTLE, TECOP, VUCA), risk register and risk report
k-11.2-identify-risks.notes: Identify individual risks and sources of overall project risk and document characteristics; key benefit: documentation of existing risks and sources so the team can respond; performed throughout and iteratively (frequency and participation set in the risk management plan). Participants: PM, team, risk specialist, customers, external SMEs, end users, other PMs, operations managers, stakeholders, organisational risk experts - but all stakeholders should be encouraged to identify risks; involving the team builds ownership. Use a consistent risk statement format for clear, unambiguous risks. Risk owners may be nominated here and confirmed in Qualitative analysis; preliminary responses may be recorded and confirmed in Plan Risk Responses. Inputs: plan (requirements, schedule, cost, quality, resource and risk management plans; scope, schedule, cost baselines - WBS as a framework for identification); documents (assumption log, cost and duration estimates and resource requirements - ideally as ranges indicating risk, issue log, lessons learned, requirements documentation, stakeholder register - who can identify risks and act as owners); agreements (milestones, contract type, acceptance criteria, awards and penalties); procurement documentation (procurement may raise or lower risk; seller performance reports, approved changes, inspections); EEFs (published material, commercial risk databases and checklists, academic studies, benchmarking, industry studies); OPAs (project files with actual data, process controls, risk statement formats, checklists from similar projects). Tools: expert judgment (account for experts' bias); data gathering - brainstorming (comprehensive list, often with multidisciplinary outside experts, free-form or structured, RBS categories as a framework, ensure ideas are clearly described), checklists (based on history; quick, but never exhaustive - must not replace proper identification; explore items not on the list; review and prune regularly), interviews (trust and confidentiality); data analysis - root cause analysis (threats from a problem statement such as 'delayed', opportunities from a benefit statement such as 'early delivery'), assumption and constraint analysis (threats from inaccurate, unstable, inconsistent or incomplete assumptions; opportunities from removing or relaxing constraints), SWOT analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats; broadens identification with internally generated risks; opportunities from strengths, threats from weaknesses; strengths may offset threats, weaknesses may hinder opportunities), document analysis (uncertainty, ambiguity or inconsistency in documents indicate risk); facilitation; prompt lists (predetermined list of risk categories to stimulate ideas: lowest RBS level for individual risks; PESTLE - political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental; TECOP - technical, environmental, commercial, operational, political; VUCA - volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity - for sources of overall risk); meetings (risk workshop, usually with brainstorming, skilled facilitator, right participants - sponsor, SMEs, sellers, customer representatives on larger projects). Outputs: risk register (results of later risk processes are recorded here too): list of identified risks with unique IDs and structured statements distinguishing cause, risk and effect; potential risk owners; list of potential responses; optional data - short title, category, status, causes, effects, risk triggers (events or conditions indicating a risk is about to occur), WBS reference, timing (when identified, when it might occur, when it may cease to matter, action deadline). Risk report (developed progressively; later processes add results): sources of overall risk with the most important drivers of exposure; summary of individual risks - numbers of threats and opportunities, distribution across categories, metrics and trends. Document updates: assumption log, issue log, lessons learned. Data flow (Figure 11-7): procurement documentation from 12.1, agreements from 12.2.

k-11.3-qualitative.title: 11.3 Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis: bias, data quality, probability and impact, other parameters, categorisation, P-I matrix, bubble charts, risk owners
k-11.3-qualitative.notes: Prioritise individual risks for further analysis or action by assessing probability, impact and other characteristics; key benefit: focus on high-priority risks; performed throughout (in agile often before each iteration). Assessments are subjective, so identify and manage participants' risk attitudes and correct for bias (a key facilitator role); evaluate the quality of available risk information. Establishes relative priorities for Plan Risk Responses, assigns a risk owner to each risk (responsible for planning and ensuring implementation of the response) and lays the foundation for Quantitative analysis if required. Inputs: risk management plan (roles, budgets, schedule activities, categories/RBS, probability and impact definitions, P-I matrix, thresholds - if missing, develop here and get sponsor approval); documents (assumption log, risk register, stakeholder register - potential owners); EEFs (industry studies, published material); OPAs (information from similar projects). Tools: expert judgment (often via facilitated workshops or interviews; consider bias); interviews (structured or semi-structured, trust and confidentiality); data analysis - risk data quality assessment (accuracy and reliability of risk data; e.g., questionnaire on completeness, objectivity, relevancy, timeliness with a weighted average score; gather better data if unacceptable), risk probability and impact assessment (likelihood; effect on schedule, cost, quality, performance - negative for threats, positive for opportunities; explore differing perceptions; record justifying assumptions; use the plan's definitions; low-probability, low-impact risks go on a watch list), assessment of other parameters - urgency (time within which a response must be implemented; short = high urgency), proximity (time before the risk could affect objectives; short = high proximity), dormancy (time after occurrence before impact is discovered; short = low dormancy), manageability, controllability, detectability (ease of detecting occurrence), connectivity (links to other risks), strategic impact, propinquity (degree a risk is perceived to matter by stakeholders); facilitation; risk categorisation (by source/RBS, area affected/WBS, phase, budget, roles, common root causes - focuses responses on the most exposed areas and enables generic responses for groups); data representation - probability and impact matrix (grid dividing risks into priority groups; separate matrices per objective, or combine assessments, or take the highest priority across objectives), hierarchical charts for more than two parameters, e.g., bubble chart (Figure 11-10: detectability on x, proximity on y, bubble size = impact value; large bubbles in the high-proximity/low-detectability area are unacceptable, small bubbles in the opposite area acceptable); meetings (risk workshop to review risks, assess probability, impact and other parameters, categorise, prioritise, allocate risk owners, confirm scales, record new risks). Outputs (documents only): assumption log, issue log, risk register (probability and impact assessments, priority level or score, risk owner, urgency, category, watch list), risk report (most important risks, prioritised list of all risks, summary conclusion).

k-11.4-quantitative-intro.title: 11.4 Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis: when it is used, inputs
k-11.4-quantitative-intro.notes: Numerically analyse the combined effect of identified individual risks and other uncertainty on overall objectives; key benefit: quantifies overall project risk exposure and supports response planning; not required on every project but performed throughout where used. Needs high-quality risk data and a sound scope, schedule and cost baseline, usually specialised software and modelling expertise, and extra time and cost; use is specified in the risk management plan; most appropriate for large or complex, strategically important, contractually required or stakeholder-required cases. It is the only reliable method to assess overall project risk by evaluating the aggregated effect of all individual risks and other uncertainty. Uses risks assessed in Qualitative analysis as significant; outputs feed Plan Risk Responses; may be repeated after response planning to test response effectiveness. Inputs: plan (risk management plan - whether required, resources, frequency; scope, schedule and cost baselines as starting points); documents (assumption log - assumptions and constraints may be modelled; basis of estimates - purpose, classification, accuracy, methodology, source reflected in modelled variability; cost estimates; cost forecasts - ETC, EAC, BAC, TCPI compared with results to find confidence levels; duration estimates; milestone list - schedule targets; resource requirements; risk register; risk report; schedule forecasts); EEFs (industry studies, published material); OPAs (similar completed projects). Expert judgment: translating risk information into numeric model inputs, choosing representations of uncertainty, modelling techniques and tools, interpreting outputs. (Tools continue on PDF 469.)
